subsection.title: Solve Absolute Value Equations
subsection.p: As we prepare to solve absolute value equations, we review our definition of absolute value.

note.p: The absolute value of a number is its distance from zero on the number line.
The absolute value of a number n is written as $$|n|$$ and $$|n| \geq 0$$ for all numbers.
Absolute values are always greater than or equal to zero.

subsection.p: We learned that both a number and its opposite are the same distance from zero on the number line. Since they have the same distance from zero, they have the same absolute value. For example:
$$\mspace{54mu}-5$$ is 5 units away from 0, so $$|-5| = 5.$$
$$\mspace{66mu} 5$$ is 5 units away from 0, so $$|5| = 5.$$
Figure 2.6 illustrates this idea.

image.alt: The figure is a number line with tick marks at negative 5, 0, and 5. The distance between negative 5 and 0 is given as 5 units, so the absolute value of negative 5 is 5. The distance between 5 and 0 is 5 units, so the absolute value of 5 is 5.
image.caption: The numbers 5 and $$-5$$ are both five units away from zero.

subsection.p: For the equation $$|x| = 5,$$ we are looking for all numbers that make this a true statement. We are looking for the numbers whose distance from zero is 5. We just saw that both 5 and $$-5$$ are five units from zero on the number line. They are the solutions to the equation.
The solution can be simplified to a single statement by writing $$x = \text{±}5.$$ This is read, “x is equal to positive or negative 5”.
We can generalize this to the following property for absolute value equations.

subsection.p: Some of our absolute value equations could be of the form $$|u| = |v|$$ where u and v are algebraic expressions. For example, $$\left| {x - 3} \right| = \left| {2x + 1} \right|.$$

How would we solve them? If two algebraic expressions are equal in absolute value, then they are either equal to each other or negatives of each other. The property for absolute value equations says that for any algebraic expression, u, and a positive real number, a, if $$|u| = a,$$ then $$u = \text{−}a$$ or $$u = a.$$

subsection.title: Solve Absolute Value Inequalities with “Less Than”
subsection.p: Let’s look now at what happens when we have an absolute value inequality. Everything we’ve learned about solving inequalities still holds, but we must consider how the absolute value impacts our work.

Again we will look at our definition of absolute value. The absolute value of a number is its distance from zero on the number line. For the equation $$|x| = 5,$$ we saw that both 5 and $$-5$$ are five units from zero on the number line. They are the solutions to the equation.

What about the inequality $$|x| \leq 5?$$ Where are the numbers whose distance is less than or equal to 5? We know $$-5$$ and 5 are both five units from zero. All the numbers between $$-5$$ and 5 are less than five units from zero. See Figure 2.7.

image.alt: The figure is a number line with negative 5, 0, and 5 displayed. There is a left bracket at negative 5 and a right bracket at 5. The distance between negative 5 and 0 is given as 5 units and the distance between 5 and 0 is given as 5 units. It illustrates that if the absolute value of x is less than or equal to 5, then negative 5 is less than or equal to x which is less than or equal to 5.

subsection.p: In a more general way, we can see that if $$|u| \leq a,$$ then $$\text{−}a \leq u \leq a.$$ See Figure 2.8.

image.alt: The figure is a number line with negative a 0, and a displayed. There is a left bracket at negative a and a right bracket at a. The distance between negative a and 0 is given as a units and the distance between a and 0 is given as a units. It illustrates that if the absolute value of u is less than or equal to a, then negative a is less than or equal to u which is less than or equal to a.

subsection.p: This result is summarized here.

note.p: For any algebraic expression, u, and any positive real number, a,
note.equation: $$\begin{array}{lccclccccl} \text{if} & & & & {|u| < a,} & & & & & {\text{then}\mspace{9mu}\text{−}a < u < a} \\ \text{if} & & & & {|u| \leq a,} & & & & & {\text{then}\mspace{9mu}\text{−}a \leq u \leq a} \end{array}$$

subsection.p: After solving an inequality, it is often helpful to check some points to see if the solution makes sense. The graph of the solution divides the number line into three sections. Choose a value in each section and substitute it in the original inequality to see if it makes the inequality true or not. While this is not a complete check, it often helps verify the solution.

subsection.title: Solve Absolute Value Inequalities with “Greater Than”
subsection.p: What happens for absolute value inequalities that have “greater than”? Again we will look at our definition of absolute value. The absolute value of a number is its distance from zero on the number line.

We started with the inequality $$|x| \leq 5.$$ We saw that the numbers whose distance is less than or equal to five from zero on the number line were $$-5$$ and 5 and all the numbers between $$-5$$ and 5. See Figure 2.9.

image.alt: The figure is a number line with negative 5, 0, and 5 displayed. There is a right bracket at negative 5 that has shading to its right and a right bracket at 5 with shading to its left. It illustrates that if the absolute value of x is less than or equal to 5, then negative 5 is less than or equal to x is less than or equal to 5.

subsection.p: Now we want to look at the inequality $$|x| \geq 5.$$ Where are the numbers whose distance from zero is greater than or equal to five?

Again both $$-5$$ and 5 are five units from zero and so are included in the solution. Numbers whose distance from zero is greater than five units would be less than $$-5$$ and greater than 5 on the number line. See Figure 2.10.

image.alt: The figure is a number line with negative 5, 0, and 5 displayed. There is a right bracket at negative 5 that has shading to its left and a left bracket at 5 with shading to its right. The distance between negative 5 and 0 is given as 5 units and the distance between 5 and 0 is given as 5 units. It illustrates that if the absolute value of x is greater than or equal to 5, then x is less than or equal to negative 5 or x is greater than or equal to 5.

subsection.p: In a more general way, we can see that if $$|u| \geq a,$$ then $$u \leq \text{−}a$$ or $$u \geq a.$$ See Figure 2.11.

image.alt: The figure is a number line with negative a, 0, and a displayed. There is a right bracket at negative a that has shading to its left and a left bracket at a with shading to its right. The distance between negative a and 0 is given as a units and the distance between a and 0 is given as a units. It illustrates that if the absolute value of u is greater than or equal to a, then u is less than or equal to negative a or u is greater than or equal to a.

subsection.p: This result is summarized here.

note.p: For any algebraic expression, u, and any positive real number, a,
note.equation: $$\begin{array}{lcccclccccl} \text{if} & & & & & {|u| > a,} & & & & & {\text{then}\ u < - a\mspace{9mu}\text{or}\mspace{9mu} u > a} \\ \text{if} & & & & & {|u| \geq a,} & & & & & {\text{then}\ u \leq \text{−}a\mspace{9mu}\text{or}\mspace{9mu} u \geq a} \end{array}$$

subsection.title: Solve Applications with Absolute Value
subsection.p: Absolute value inequalities are often used in the manufacturing process. An item must be made with near perfect specifications. Usually there is a certain tolerance of the difference from the specifications that is allowed. If the difference from the specifications exceeds the tolerance, the item is rejected.

problem.p: The ideal diameter of a rod needed for a machine is 60 mm. The actual diameter can vary from the ideal diameter by $$0.075$$ mm. What range of diameters will be acceptable to the customer without causing the rod to be rejected?

problem.p: A chicken farm ideally produces 200,000 eggs per day. But this total can vary by as much as 25,000 eggs. What is the maximum and minimum expected production at the farm?
An organic juice bottler ideally produces 215,000 bottle per day. But this total can vary by as much as 7,500 bottles. What is the maximum and minimum expected production at the bottling company?

solution.p: The minimum to maximum expected production is 207,500 to 2,225,000 bottles

problem.p: In order to insure compliance with the law, Miguel routinely overshoots the weight of his tortillas by 0.5 gram. He just received a report that told him that he could be losing as much as $100,000 per year using this practice. He now plans to buy new equipment that guarantees the thickness of the tortilla within 0.005 inches. If the ideal thickness of the tortilla is 0.04 inches, what thickness of tortillas will be guaranteed?

At Lilly’s Bakery, the ideal weight of a loaf of bread is 24 ounces. By law, the actual weight can vary from the ideal by 1.5 ounces. What range of weight will be acceptable to the inspector without causing the bakery being fined?

solution.p: The acceptable weight is 22.5 to 25.5 ounces.
